section_summary: This section documents Allied efforts to secure former Japanese diplomatic and consular archives in Mexico, Canada, and Argentina after Japan’s surrender. Most pages comprise a detailed Buenos Aires Embassy inventory of books, registration records, correspondence, and confidential files transferred by the Swiss protecting power. The most significant Argentine records reveal Japanese propaganda subsidies, press and intelligence expenditures, diplomatic communications, trade reporting, code destruction, Embassy staffing, and relations with Axis representatives and Latin American officials during 1941–1942.

subfiles.title: The Japanese Archives
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, U.S. Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports Mexico’s acceptance of transferring Japanese diplomatic and consular archives from the Swedish protecting power to the four principal Allied powers.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith reviewed Allied instructions with Mexican Foreign Office official Campos Ortiz and explained that the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, and China intended jointly to receive the Japanese archives. Campos Ortiz distinguished the case from German archives because a Japanese government still existed and could direct the protecting power. Mexico therefore raised no objection, provided its authorized officials could consult the records.

subfiles.title: Follow-up on Japanese archives and property in Mexico
subfiles.doc_type: office memorandum; enclosure to despatch no. 27,641
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, U.S. Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.to: Embassy files / U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Records British instructions for disposing of Japanese archives, property, and funds and arrangements for an Allied meeting.
subfiles.summary: The British ambassador reported instructions to take over the archives jointly and send them through the American representative to Washington, while liquidating movable and real property. Messersmith lacked parallel instructions and doubted Mexico would permit Japanese funds to leave the country. Counselor Geist arranged a December 4 meeting with the British, Soviet, and Chinese chiefs of mission, and the Swedish minister confirmed that Mexico’s reply allowed delivery of the archives.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese archives and property in Canada
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, signed Byrnes
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo, for George Atcheson Jr.
subfiles.about: Requests Japanese instructions authorizing the Swiss to deliver archives and property in Canada to the U.S. ambassador.
subfiles.summary: Ottawa reported that the Canadian Department of External Affairs did not intend to assume custody of Japanese archives and property. Canada would accept instructions from the Japanese government directing the Swiss protecting power to transfer them to the U.S. ambassador, and SCAP was asked to arrange this.

subfiles.title: A Cursory Examination of Former Japanese Diplomatic and Consular Archives in Argentina
subfiles.from: John M. Cabot, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Transmits seventeen inventories prepared after a preliminary examination of former Japanese diplomatic and consular records in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Second Secretary Gerald Warner examined the transferred archives for two weeks, inventorying twelve boxes, a steel cabinet, three sealed trunks, and Japanese registration cards. Cabot identified the trunks, account records, communications, and registration files as the most promising materials for further investigation and possible shipment to Washington. The Swiss retained current registration cards for protection work, while Allied and Argentine authorities received access to the stored archives.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 1
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 1 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists eighty-six Japanese, French, Spanish, and English books found in the first wooden box.
subfiles.summary: The box contained Japanese legal, diplomatic, economic, geographic, and commercial works, along with reference books on Japan and international law. Its Western-language holdings concentrated on Uruguayan and Argentine law, history, diplomacy, and geography, with additional works on Paraguay and Latin America. Allied authorities examined it on November 19, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 2
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 2 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists eighty-three volumes in the second wooden box.
subfiles.summary: The box included a twenty-volume Japanese financial history and French, Spanish, and English works on China, Japan, the Soviet Union, Latin America, communism, economics, and international affairs. Several books concerned Japanese expansion, Manchuria, Buddhism, and the position of second-generation Japanese. It was examined on November 19, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 3
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 3 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists ninety-three non-Japanese-language volumes in the third wooden box.
subfiles.summary: The box contained Portuguese works on Japan and extensive Spanish-language collections of treaties, laws, financial legislation, and diplomatic records from Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Latin America. Allied authorities examined it on November 20, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 4
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 4 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists eighty-four volumes in the fourth wooden box.
subfiles.summary: Japanese holdings emphasized diplomatic history, immigration, foreigners, finance, Manchuria, colonies, dictionaries, and imperial ceremonies. French, Spanish, and English books added treaty collections, diplomatic manuals, military studies, Uruguayan history, etiquette, and Japanese commercial law. The examination occurred on November 21, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 5
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 5 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists 115 books and maps in the fifth wooden box.
subfiles.summary: The multilingual collection ranged from treaties, dictionaries, and Japanese literature to Argentine and Uruguayan codes, public administration, economics, foreign policy, and military history. English books focused heavily on Japan’s diplomacy, expansion, art, and Pacific strategy. The box also held maps of First World War operations in Belgium, France, and Germany and was examined on November 21, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 6
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 6 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists seventy-four Japanese volumes in the sixth wooden box.
subfiles.summary: The holdings consisted of treaty series, international-affairs yearbooks, dictionaries, works on maritime law, banking, international law, and sericulture, and illustrated works on Japanese art and imperial ceremonies. One album documented the Argentine economic mission’s 1940 visit to Japan. The box was examined on November 21, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 7
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 7 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Records sixty-nine volumes of a Japanese Foreign Office treaty compilation packed with January 1944 newspapers.
subfiles.summary: The seventh box consisted of the three-volume, multi-part Joyaku Isan treaty compilation issued by the Japanese Foreign Office Treaty Bureau. Old copies of La Prensa, La Nación, and Boletín Avisador Mercantil served as packing material. Allied authorities examined the box on November 22, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 8
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 8 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists eighty-nine predominantly Japanese treaty, trade, and foreign-affairs volumes in box no. 8.
subfiles.summary: The collection covered Soviet, Chinese, European, and international treaties; foreign customs, exchange controls, landownership rules, and trade-promotion systems; and economic conditions affecting Japanese residents in Brazil. It also included Washington Conference records, Sino-Japanese agreements, and English-language arms-limitation documents. The header’s reference to box no. 1 is an evident error for box no. 8.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 9
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 9 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Inventories Japanese diplomatic, legal, reference, and cultural works in the ninth wooden box.
subfiles.summary: The box held early Japanese diplomatic correspondence, law compilations, treaty materials, commercial studies, sea-warfare regulations, and investigations concerning Manchuria and China. German, French, Spanish, and English reference works included diplomatic dictionaries, Argentine and Uruguayan laws, Japanese constitutional and commercial law, education, fine arts, and Manchukuo. It was examined on November 23, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 10
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 10 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists one hundred volumes and several photographs in the tenth wooden box.
subfiles.summary: Japanese materials included treaty collections, encyclopedias, consular lists, and photographs of ministers Uchiyama, Yamasaki, and Nakamura and the training ship Kaiwo Maru. Most Spanish works concerned Argentine university law courses, education, government reports, customs, aviation, dictionaries, Paraguay, Panama, and Uruguay. Allied authorities examined the box on November 23, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 11
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 11 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists ninety-seven volumes in the eleventh wooden box.
subfiles.summary: This box combined Japanese dictionaries and studies of Latin American conditions with extensive Argentine history, politics, economics, biography, and diplomacy. English books addressed Latin America, hemispheric strategy, the Pacific War, democracy, Moscow, and wartime operations, while German works concerned Argentina, South America, and Japan in East Asia. It was examined on November 24, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of wooden box no. 12
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 12 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese registration records, legal compilations, maritime files, dictionaries, and regional studies in box no. 12.
subfiles.summary: The most important contents were annual Mibun Todokesho registration files for 1918–1944 and thirteen volumes of current Japanese laws. Maritime files included seamen’s law, ship-safety regulations, and records identifying the Himeli Maru’s ownership and captains. The box also contained works on Catamarca, Chaco, Misiones, Iguazú, Patagonia, and Paraguay and was examined on November 24, 1945.

subfiles.title: Contents of steel cabinet nos. 83/181
subfiles.doc_type: archive inventory; enclosure no. 13 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Tabulates non-confidential Embassy and consular correspondence entrusted to the Swiss Legation.
subfiles.summary: The cabinet held 105 volumes of Embassy correspondence from 1932 and 1936–1943, including communications with Tokyo, Paraguay, Uruguay, other posts, the diplomatic corps, and Argentine ministries. Eight consular volumes contained certified signatures, translations, nationality and identity certificates, and government correspondence. The listed registry of Japanese residents in Argentina was missing when the cabinet was examined on November 29, 1945.

subfiles.title: Contents of trunk no. I
subfiles.doc_type: confidential archive survey; enclosure no. 14 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Summarizes confidential Japanese Embassy files, especially propaganda, press, intelligence, entertainment, and operating expenditures.
subfiles.summary: Folder 1 documented destruction of telegrams and code books, Japanese trade reporting, and subsidies or payments to newspapers, agencies, publicists, investigators, translators, and Embassy employees. The accounts show efforts to influence Axis-aligned publications, monitor communism and foreign media, cultivate Argentine and Paraguayan officials and journalists, and maintain radio and news services. Folder 4 recorded large expenditures for Embassy furnishings, rent, liquor, and international cables during late 1941 and early 1942. The sealed trunk was examined on November 30, 1945.

subfiles.title: Contents of trunk no. II
subfiles.doc_type: confidential archive survey; enclosure no. 15 to despatch no. 1557
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires / Allied examining authorities
subfiles.about: Inventories economic reports, code-custody notices, personnel data, premises, vehicles, and trade files in the second sealed trunk.
subfiles.summary: Folder 29 contained late-1941 economic and diplomatic reporting on Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay, Valparaíso, Embassy personnel movements, and the status of telegraphic codes. Folder 30 included a detailed January 1942 roster of Argentine, Spanish, German, and Japanese employees, their duties, salaries, and employment dates, together with reports on Embassy cars and leased premises. Folders 31–33 consisted mainly of Argentine trade statistics, central-bank and finance-ministry reports, and Business Conditions in Argentina. The inventory begins Folder 34 at page 377 and continues beyond this section.
